options: Tiny pores on a leaf surface that open and close
The hard part inside a seed
questions.explanation: Stomata are small pores, or openings, on the surface of leaves and stems that can open and close.
questions.misconception: Stomata are not roots, petals, or seed parts; they are tiny adjustable pores on the leaf surface used for gas exchange.

questions.prompt: What happens at an open stoma?
options: Carbon dioxide comes in and oxygen goes out
No gas ever moves through it
questions.explanation: Through an open stoma, a plant takes in carbon dioxide to power photosynthesis and releases oxygen that it makes.
questions.misconception: Some learners reverse this thinking it works like animal lungs. But plants take carbon dioxide in and give oxygen out through stomata.

questions.prompt: What controls whether a stoma is open or closed?
options: Two guard cells that build apart, or meet together
questions.explanation: Each stoma is framed by two guard cells. They swell and bend apart to open the pore, and relax to bring them together and close it.
questions.misconception: It is not a root, petal, or seed that controls this - it is the two guard cells beside each pore that swell and bend.

questions.prompt: Why might a plant close its stomata on a hot, dry day?
options: To save water by stopping it from escaping
questions.explanation: When open, the pores lose water. On a hot, dry day the plant closes its stomata to stop losing too much water.
questions.misconception: Closing is not for letting in heat, making oxygen, or pollinators. It is a water-saving move even though it means taking in less carbon dioxide.
